title: Week 1 Mastery Quiz — How We Know the Past

questions.prompt: A handwritten diary entry created during an event is best classified as which kind of evidence?
choices: Primary source
Secondary source
Historical claim
Corroboration
questions.explanation: A primary source was created during the period or event being studied. Its closeness to the event makes it valuable evidence, but it still must be evaluated for purpose, perspective, context, and limits.

questions.prompt: A historian compares two eyewitness accounts with meeting minutes and a newspaper report. Which historical-thinking practice is the historian using most directly?
choices: Periodization
Corroboration
Memorization
Prediction
questions.explanation: Corroboration means checking one source against independent evidence to identify agreement, contradiction, and uncertainty.

questions.prompt: Which question is most useful for contextualizing a source?
choices: Is the source interesting?
Is the source longer than the others?
What conditions, values, and events shaped the source when it was created?
Does the source agree with my first impression?
questions.explanation: Contextualization places evidence within the conditions, values, institutions, and events of its time rather than judging it outside that setting.

questions.prompt: Two witnesses agree that a vote occurred but disagree about why several people opposed it. What is the strongest historical conclusion?
choices: One witness must be lying.
The disagreement makes both accounts useless.
The motive is already proven because both witnessed the event.
The occurrence of the vote is better corroborated than the disputed motive.
questions.explanation: Agreement can strengthen one part of a claim while disagreement preserves uncertainty about another. Historians separate what the evidence supports strongly from what remains disputed.

questions.prompt: Which statement about bias is most accurate?
choices: Bias can shape what a source includes or omits, so perspective must be analyzed rather than treated as automatic disqualification.
Any biased source must be discarded.
Only primary sources contain bias.
A source that claims neutrality cannot contain bias.
questions.explanation: Perspective can shape every kind of source. Bias is a reason to examine origin, audience, purpose, and limits—not a reason to discard evidence automatically.

questions.prompt: Which statement is a defensible historical claim rather than an unsupported assertion?
choices: The loudest witness was obviously the most accurate.
Because three independent records agree that the meeting ended at 8:00 p.m., that conclusion is better supported than a single conflicting recollection.
The oldest surviving source must always be correct.
If evidence is incomplete, historians cannot make any claims.
questions.explanation: A defensible historical claim identifies evidence and explains why that evidence supports the conclusion while remaining open to limits or contrary evidence.

questions.prompt: A map shows where six witnesses were standing during a public meeting. What can the map most responsibly help a historian evaluate?
choices: Which witness had the best personality
Whether every witness remembered accurately
How location and line of sight may have shaped what each person could observe
Which political position was morally correct
questions.explanation: Spatial evidence can help explain differences in observation. It cannot by itself prove memory accuracy, motive, personality, or moral correctness.

questions.prompt: Which practice best protects against overclaiming when evidence is incomplete?
choices: Ignore contradictory evidence
Choose the account with the most dramatic language
State the conclusion as certain so readers will trust it
Name the uncertainty, explain the strongest evidence, and identify what additional evidence would help
questions.explanation: Strong historical reasoning distinguishes evidence from inference and communicates uncertainty instead of pretending the record is more complete than it is.

questions.prompt: A speech was written to persuade voters. Why can it still be useful historical evidence?
choices: Persuasive sources are automatically factual.
Its purpose and audience can reveal what the speaker wanted voters to believe, especially when its factual claims are checked against other evidence.
Its persuasive purpose proves every opposing source false.
A speech is useful only when the historian agrees with it.
questions.explanation: Purpose is part of a source's evidentiary value. A persuasive source can reveal arguments, priorities, audiences, and assumptions while factual claims still require corroboration.

questions.prompt: Which sequence represents the strongest method for evaluating a disputed historical claim?
choices: Choose a source, summarize it, stop
Search only for evidence that confirms the first source
Define the question, source and contextualize evidence, corroborate across independent records, then make a qualified claim
Count how many sources exist without examining who created them
questions.explanation: Reliable historical inquiry begins with a clear question, evaluates source origin and context, compares independent evidence, and then makes a claim proportionate to the evidence.

shortResponse.prompt: Using at least two specific ideas from this week, explain how a historian can build a trustworthy account when surviving evidence is incomplete or disputed. Your response must distinguish evidence from inference and identify one limitation or uncertainty.
shortResponse.exemplar: Full-credit work makes a defensible claim, accurately uses at least two Week 1 concepts such as sourcing, contextualization, corroboration, bias, spatial evidence, or qualified claims, explains how those concepts strengthen reliability, and identifies one remaining uncertainty or additional source that would help.
